::: {.lead}
A small studio is making *Lantern Keeper*, a mobile game about a lantern
spirit in a dark forest. The rules are ready: tap to float, collect
fireflies. But the game still feels empty. It needs pictures, music, sounds,
words and a story. Players meet a game through these **media**. This course
is about how game media are planned, made and protected. In this first
lesson you learn what digital media are, how all parts of a game (the story
too) work together for the player, which jobs media do in a game, and how a
team makes media step by step. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary digital-media multimedia elemental-tetrad mechanics aesthetics player-experience feedback asset production-pipeline pre-production >}}

## 1.1 What digital media are

A player of *Lantern Keeper* reads a line of text, sees a painted forest,
hears a chime and watches a short scene, all in one minute. A **medium**
(plural *media*) is a way to share content: writing, pictures, sound,
moving pictures (@fig-annotated).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Digital media"}
**Digital media** are text, images, audio, video, animation and interactive
content stored as numbers, so that a computer can store, edit, copy and
send them. A work that combines several types is **multimedia**.
:::

Games use all six types:

- **text**: dialogue, menus, item names, subtitles;
- **images**: characters, backgrounds, icons;
- **audio**: music, sound effects, voices;
- **video**: cut-scenes and trailers;
- **animation**: pictures or poses in a sequence that make movement;
- **interactive media**: content that answers the player. The game itself
  is the best example.

Images are stored in two ways: as a grid of pixels (a **raster** image, for
photos and painted art) or as shapes (**vector** graphics, for logos and
buttons that stay sharp at any size).

![A screen of a mobile game: each number marks one media element.](images/annotated-screen.png){#fig-annotated width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — The media of one level"}
In one level of *Lantern Keeper*:

1. **Text:** "Light the lanterns before sunrise!"
2. **Images and animation:** the painted forest, the floating spirit.
3. **Audio:** soft piano music and a chime for each firefly.
4. **Video:** a short scene of the village at the end of the level.
5. **Interactive media:** the player taps, and the spirit floats up.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting that the game itself is a medium. The rules that answer the
player are interactive media, the one type that films and books do not
have.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Six types in your game"}
Choose a game on your phone. Write one example of each of the six types of
media from this game.

*Your result:* six examples.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "Text: the names of the cards. Images: the
characters. Audio: the music of the menu. Video: the intro scene.
Animation: the hero running. Interactive media: the game reacts to my
taps." Check: six different types, each with a real example from the game.
:::
:::

## 1.2 The game as a composite medium

A game combines all types of media with something that no other medium
has: rules that the player acts on. The designer Jesse Schell describes a
game as four basic elements, the **elemental tetrad** (@fig-tetrad).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — The elemental tetrad"}
- **Mechanics:** the rules, what the player can do and what happens then.
- **Story:** the events of the game, written in advance or created by
  play.
- **Aesthetics:** how the game looks, sounds and feels.
- **Technology:** the device, the engine, the screen and the speakers.

All four are equally important. Game media succeed when they make the
planned **player experience** stronger.
:::

![The elemental tetrad (after Schell). All four elements together create the player's experience.](images/tetrad.png){#fig-tetrad width=62%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — The tetrad of Tide Runner"}
*Tide Runner* is a surfing game for phones.

1. **Mechanics:** swipe up to jump over a wave; a missed wave costs speed.
2. **Story:** a young surfer must bring medicine to an island before the
   storm.
3. **Aesthetics:** bright sea colours, steel-drum music, a splash for each
   jump.
4. **Technology:** a phone in landscape; simple water effects so that old
   phones keep 60 frames per second.
5. The planned experience, *fast and joyful*, comes from all four. Slow,
   sad music would break it, even with the same rules.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that *aesthetics* means *graphics*. Aesthetics are everything the
player's senses meet: pictures, but also sound, music, vibration and the
rhythm of animation.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/juice-it.html" poster="sims/juice-it.png" title="Juice It: same mechanics, different media" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Juice It"}
Open the **Juice It** mini-game above (or scan its QR code). The rules
never change: tap to jump.

1. Play 30 seconds with all media layers off.
2. Switch the layers on one at a time: sound effects, music, particles,
   camera shake, story. Play a little after each one.
3. Choose one word for the experience at the start, and one at the end.

*Your result:* the two words, and the layer that changed the experience
most.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "At the start: boring. At the end: exciting. The
sound effects changed it most, because every jump and star now gives
feedback." The rules stayed the same; only the media changed the
experience.
:::
:::

## 1.3 The jobs of game media

In a good game, every media element has a job. Five jobs, or
**functions**, appear again and again (@fig-functions).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.3 — The functions of game media"}
- **Feedback:** what happened because of my action? (a chime and a flash
  for a coin)
- **Guidance:** where should I go? (a glowing door, a lit path)
- **Mood:** how should this moment feel? (slow music in a sad scene)
- **Story:** what is happening? (dialogue, a cut-scene, a broken statue)
- **Identity:** which game is this? (a theme tune, a logo, a clear art
  style)

One element often has several functions.
:::

![One coin, three functions: the sound sets the mood, the "+10" gives feedback, and the next coins guide the player.](images/media-functions.png){#fig-functions width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — The splash of Tide Runner"}
Each jump in *Tide Runner* makes a splash and a white spray.

1. **Feedback:** the player knows at once that the jump worked.
2. **Mood:** the bright splash feels fresh and joyful.
3. **Identity:** players know the game by its splash sound.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Describing instead of explaining. "There is music in the menu" only
describes. "The slow music in the menu makes the player calm before play
begins" names the element, its job and its effect on the player.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Sound off"}
Play a game you know for one minute with the sound off.

1. What is missing? Name one sound and its job (feedback, guidance, mood,
   story or identity).
2. How does the game help a player who cannot hear (for example a flash or
   a vibration)?

*Your result:* one sound with its job, and one answer.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "The hit sound is missing: its job is feedback,
so I do not notice when I lose health. The game also flashes the screen
red, so a player who cannot hear still gets the feedback." Check: a real
sound, its job, and one other channel that does the same job.
:::
:::

## 1.4 The creative production pipeline

A team does not make game media in one step. Professional teams follow a
**production pipeline** with three main stages (@fig-pipeline).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.4 — Production pipeline"}
- **Pre-production:** planning: the idea, the story, the script, the
  storyboard, a style guide, the time plan and the budget.
- **Production:** making the **assets**: drawing, modelling, animating,
  composing music, recording voices and sounds, filming.
- **Post-production:** finishing: editing, mixing the sound, correcting
  colours, exporting the files in the formats the game needs (for example
  PNG for pictures, Ogg for sounds), then testing them in the game.
:::

![The creative production pipeline. Testing often sends work back to an earlier stage.](images/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=94%}

This course follows the same order: story and scripts (lectures 2–4) and
storyboards (lectures 5–6) are pre-production; sound, music and video
(lectures 7–11) are production and post-production. Intellectual property
(lectures 12–13) matters at every stage, because every picture, sound and
text has an owner.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.4 — One sound through the pipeline"}
The splash of *Tide Runner*:

1. **Pre-production:** the plan asks for "a short, bright splash, under one
   second".
2. **Production:** the sound designer records water in a bowl three times,
   so that the jumps do not all sound the same.
3. **Post-production:** the recordings are cut, made equally loud and saved
   as small Ogg files.
4. **Testing:** a tester says that the splash hides the music. The sound
   goes back to post-production for a new mix.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Starting with production. Without a plan, assets do not fit together, and
a lot of work is made again.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Make one small asset"}
Make a coin icon for a game, and follow the three stages.

1. **Pre-production:** write a one-line plan, for example "a gold coin with
   a star, round, easy to see on a dark background".
2. **Production:** draw it in Paint (or another tool).
3. **Post-production:** save it as a PNG file with a clear name, for
   example `icon_coin_v1.png`.

*Your result:* the one-line plan and the PNG file.

::: {.check}
A good result: a one-line plan that says the shape, the colour and where
the icon is used; a simple drawing that follows it; and a file such as
`icon_coin_v1.png`. Check: the file name says what the asset is and its
version.
:::
:::

## Case study: Lantern Keeper's media plan

*Lantern Keeper* is a made-up mobile game: a lantern spirit floats through
a dark forest, collects fireflies and must light the village lanterns
before sunrise. The team must plan its media: a 2-minute music loop, a
firefly chime with three variations, a logo for the store page, a painted
forest background and a 30-second trailer. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses this plan. The mini-game below is a small version
of the game: switch the four elements of the tetrad on and off and see what
the player loses.

{{< sim file="sims/lantern-keeper.html" poster="sims/lantern-keeper.png" title="Lantern Keeper: switch the tetrad on and off" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses*, 3rd ed., Chapters 1–4
(the designer, the experience, the game and the elemental tetrad).

## Exercises

1. Name the six types of digital media in games. Give one example of each
   from a game you know.
2. A game logo must appear on an app icon and on a big poster. Raster or
   vector? Why?
3. Name the four elements of the elemental tetrad.
4. Which element of the tetrad is the story? Give one example of how a
   story changes the player's experience.
5. Why is aesthetics not the same as graphics?
6. Name the five functions of game media.
7. A glowing door shows where to go. Which function is this?
8. Put each task in a stage of the pipeline: writing the script; mixing
   the music; recording a voice; drawing the storyboard; exporting a
   trailer.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Text (subtitles), images (characters), audio (music), video
   (cut-scene), animation (a walk), interactive media (the game itself).
2. Vector: it stays sharp at every size.
3. Mechanics, story, aesthetics, technology.
4. Story. For example: in Tide Runner the medicine must reach the island
   before the storm, so every missed wave feels urgent.
5. Aesthetics include everything the senses meet: also sound, music,
   vibration and rhythm.
6. Feedback, guidance, mood, story, identity.
7. Guidance.
8. Pre-production: the script, the storyboard; production: recording a
   voice; post-production: mixing the music, exporting a trailer.
:::
